title: Asking Work to Stop: A Flag Cannot Wake a Sleeper, and a Callback Must Not Outlive What It Captured

questions.question: A worker polls a stop flag between 10 ms sleeps. How long after the request does it stop, measured?
options: Under a microsecond
Exactly 10 ms
Immediately, since the flag is atomic
A median of 3.27 ms and a worst of about 9.3 ms
questions.explanation: It notices only when it next wakes, so the delay is up to the whole interval. A wait the request itself wakes had a median of 72 us. Polling is not wrong, it is slow in proportion to its sleep.

questions.question: stop.request_stop() sets a flag. A consumer is asleep inside queue.pop_for with a 1500 ms wait. What happens?
options: Nothing: a flag is something to look at and a sleeping thread is not looking
It wakes and exits at once
The thread is killed
The queue closes itself
questions.explanation: It sleeps until an item arrives or the wait ends. A StopCallback that calls queue.close() is the answer. Measured: three consumers asleep, request_stop(), all three returned closed within 0 ms.

questions.question: A loop checks a stop flag every 64 iterations, and the request is made at iteration 100. At which iteration does it stop, counted?
options: 128, the next multiple of 64 at or after the request
It never stops
questions.explanation: How often a loop looks is how fast it stops. Checked every 1: 100. Every 1000: 1000. Every 100000: 100000. A loop that never looks cannot be stopped, which is what cooperative means.

questions.question: A StopCallback is registered after request_stop() has already been called. What happens?
options: It runs at once, where it is constructed
It throws
It never runs, since the request is over
It runs on the next request
questions.explanation: Registering late cannot miss the request. The constructor checks the stopped flag under the same lock the requester copies the list under, so the action runs exactly once whichever side got there first.

questions.question: Why does ~StopCallback lock the run mutex after removing its entry?
options: To count callbacks
To make the list thread safe
To wait for a request that is running callbacks now
To notify the requester
questions.explanation: What the action captured is not destroyed while the action is still using it. Measured, forced: a callback held open, its owner destroyed on another thread. The destructor waited, and the callback finished before it did.

questions.question: The requester takes the run mutex before copying the callback list. What would go wrong if it copied first?
options: Nothing
A destructor could erase its entry, find nothing running, and return, while the requester held a copy of the list that still included it and then ran it against memory that is gone
The list would be copied twice
The callbacks would run in the wrong order
questions.explanation: Taking the lock first means a destructor either finds the list without its entry or waits for the run. There is no moment where a callback is about to run and its owner has gone.
